body.text: Public hearings for Victoria's royal commission examining allegations of corruption on government building sites have begun in Melbourne.
It comes as the state's election campaign enters the final three-week stretch ahead of polling day on November 28.

The hearings held in private

The commissioner may determine that a hearing should be conducted in private, and there are a range of reasons for it.

In some cases, there might be vulnerable witnesses who need protection. In others, evidence might relate to a current police investigation, and having it livestreamed (and blogged) could prejudice a future criminal trial.
Of course, the hearings wouldn’t be very private if we knew who was interviewed, so we’ll remain in the dark on that front.
Labor in the firing line with royal commission

Journalist Nick McKenzie, who first aired allegations of corruption on Victoria's major construction projects, said this block of hearings could "seal the fate of Labor", weeks out from the state election.

"It's actually an extraordinary way for the royal commission to start because front and centre is Jacinta Allan and her office," he told 774 ABC Melbourne. "The allegation is this: that Jacinta Allan's office, when she was Transport Infrastructure Minister intervened in that project in an allegedly improper or even corrupt way."
"It's actually an extraordinary way for the royal commission to start because front and centre is Jacinta Allan and her office," he told 774 ABC Melbourne.
"The allegation is this: that Jacinta Allan's office, when she was Transport Infrastructure Minister intervened in that project in an allegedly improper or even corrupt way."
In June, then-premier Jacinta Allan insisted the government had acted "quickly and strongly" to allegations of criminal infiltration of government building sites.
Royal commission takes a recess
Most of the morning has been providing background on the royal commission itself, and on the Gap Road level crossing project in Sunbury.
We'll have more when the commission returns from its morning break.
More key firms identified
Mr Young says much of the work at Gap Road was done by subcontractors and labour hire firms.
Zoom Recruitment, STA Traffic Management and Wagstaff Piling are named as some of the firms working on the Sunbury site.
The Labour Hire Authority this year cancelled the licence of B K Labour Hire after an investigation by LHA and high-profile arrests by Victoria Police’s Hawk Taskforce at the company’s headquarters.
More background on the Gap Road project
Mr Young stresses the occupation of a rail line and shutdown of the Sunbury line came with huge financial costs, with the occupation not easily able to be rescheduled.
He spends some time going over the agreement signed by the Rail Network Alliance regarding the project, which encouraged cooperation between the different firms.

Two unions had an interest in the work: The Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union (CFMEU) and the Australian Workers' Union (AWU), and the two unions were competing for coverage of work sites in Victoria.

Mr Young reads a report describing the contest between the unions with the high number of infrastructure projects in the state, and analysis that the CFMEU had made in-roads into traditional AWU territory.
Key Event
Background on the level crossing removal in Sunbury
The removal of the Gap Road level crossing was announced by the government in 2018, and was done by removing the road under the railway track and building a bridge.

The choice was made by Major Transport Infrastructure Authority (MTIA) to deliver the project through a separate partnership known as the Rail Network Alliance rather than the existing level cross removal team.
The target cost for the works was $110 million, and the planned completion date was the April 23, 2023.
The critical works were done during a shutdown of the Sunbury line in June 2022. While an occupation of the line lasts, trains cannot run on the line and traffic is blocked.
Warnings about witnesses
Before we get into what occurred at Gap Road, Mr Young notes there will be witnesses who have been compelled to appear.
He says it is a serious offence to threaten a witness or punish them for appearing before the royal commission, and says harsh penalties apply for those who do.
"If we learn that a witness has been threatened, punished or warned off, we will ask you to protect that witness, and we will ask that the matter immediately be referred to Victoria Police," he says.
We begin on the work stoppage at Gap Road
Mr Young raises a document that was tendered in the opening hearing of the royal commission.
It is a briefing dated June 21, 2023 sent to the then-minister for transport and infrastructure, Jacinta Allan.
It raised issues observed including:
i. the pressuring of construction contractors, including through intimidatory tactics, to agree to:
ii. A. demands for additional and/or excess site staffing;
B. the use of particular persons and companies, in order to avoid industrial disputation; unions' non-acquiescence to rosters and arrangements suitable for 24/7occupations, leading to program delays;
iii. an increased proliferation of full time, non-working union delegates and Health and Safety Representatives (HSRs) with some recent appointments having limited construction experience;
iv. a concern that industrial issues are erroneously being portrayed as safety issues, with little engagement or assistance provided by WorkSafe;
v. an increase in the prevalence of inappropriate requests for higher shift/leave loading and allowances beyond the relevant EBA;
vi. an increase in the prevalence of threats of unprotected industrial action; and
vii. an increasingly apparent lack of skills and/or experience in industrial relations management amongst contractors and subcontractors.
The theme of future hearings
Mr Young says future blocks will explore the integration of organised crime into the construction industry.
He says members of organised crime were often given "large payments" for services that amounted to "little more than intimidation and menace".
Mr Young says other future hearings will deal with how government money was allocated, and how certain public projects were decided.
Key Event
The central themes of the investigation
Mr Young lists what he calls "themes" of the royal commission's investigation into corruption on government work sites.
He notes these are all allegations at this stage, and some have been denied.
Among the themes, Mr Young says:
• Union delegates were placed on sites as health and safety representatives by the CFMEU, many of whom were unelected
• Labour hire companies were used to place the delegates on sites
• Work stoppages increased following the abolition and defunding of the Australian Building and Construction Commission (ABCC) by the federal Labor government
• Contractors were left to handle issues themselves, and often resorted to "buying peace", pricing the cost of doing business into their bids
• The cost of these industrial disruptions was "shared with the state or pass to it"
What the royal commission has done so far
Counsel assisting Chris Young KC covers what the royal commission has already uncovered in its preliminary work.
Mr Young says more than 110,000 documents have already been requested by the commission, and hundreds of notices have been sent out.
Secret hearings have also been held already, with witnesses interviewed in private.
Key Event
The Gap Road project in Sunbury
The hearing today will examine the events of June 2022 at the Gap Road project in Sunbury.
The project involved the removal of a level crossing and the construction of a new rail bridge and underpass as part of the Sunbury Line Upgrade.
On June 6 and 7 in 2022, there was a work stoppage.
After a meeting at the CFMEU offices on June 7, work resumed with control of the site transferred to the union.
The royal commission will investigate what occurred, what arrangements were made, what they cost and what the government knew.
The political implications of the royal commission
Establishing the royal commission was Ben Carroll's first act as premier, a move that distanced him from predecessor Jacinta Allan.
But any hope the public would reward Carroll and Labor for calling the inquiry quickly evaporated.
The government didn't receive a poll bounce from changing leaders — it thus seems unlikely voters will reward Labor over the next fortnight if hearings expose fresh corruption claims.

The royal commission explained
The construction sites of the Victorian government's Big Build have become hotbeds for allegations of criminal wrongdoing, corruption and serious misconduct.
The Victorian government has called a royal commission into the alleged corruption, with its first hearings to begin this week.
